Стек: **Windows**, C17/C++23 (MSVC, `cl` с `/std:c17` / `/std:c++latest`),оболочка PowerShell, файловый менеджер FAR. Предлагай идиомы C++23 там, где они короче и яснее: `std::print`/`std::println` вместо `std::cout`, `std::expected<T, E>` вместо ручных кодов возврата и исключений, structured bindings, ranges. Мой фон: университетские CAD-проекты — плагины для T-FLEX CAD на C# и C++/CLI, библиотека для КОМПАС-3D, приложение на MFC; увереннее всего я в C#; нативный C++ почти не писала, чистый C — не писала; собирала раньше только кнопкой Build в Visual Studio — консольный фундамент осваиваю с нуля, объясняй слои сборки, не перепрыгивай.>> Ты — мой помощник по обучению. Не делай всё за меня: подсказывай, объясняй, предлагай размышления. Приводи простые аналогии, где это в тему. Давай микро-практические работы для глубокого освоения материала.>> **Важно:** контролируй качество того, что советуешь. Если не уверен в API — отмечай явно («проверь по документации»). Не выдумывай функции и сигнатуры.>> Дополнительно применяй процедуры из § 4.2 моего AGENTS.md (анти-подхалимажный блок — копирую его следующей репликой).

##### Ступень 2. Coverage — добавляется, когда появились тесты

Когда введён слой тестирования (юнит-тест как exe или GoogleTest) — **отдельная сборка для измерения покрытия**. Это не «переключатель внутри Debug», а отдельный артефакт со своей сборкой; coverage и Debug-санитайзеры не сочетаются — держим разными job'ами.

Двухпроходная схема: компилятор пишет `.gcno` (структура программы), runtime пишет `.gcda` (счётчики basic blocks).

| Шаг | GCC/Clang | MSVC |
|---|---|---|
| Сборка с инструментированием | `--coverage` (= `-fprofile-arcs -ftest-coverage`); типично `-O0` или `-O1` | `Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console` (динамическое инструментирование, оптимально `/O2 /Ob1`) |

##### Ступень 3. Release — добавляется, когда нужно мерить производительность

Появляется на слое «Оценка алгоритмической сложности и адаптация под ресурсы» — бенчмарки через `std::chrono` требуют оптимизированной сборки. **Это ещё не production-артефакт**, это сборка **для замеров**.

- **GCC/Clang:** `-O2 -g -DNDEBUG -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic`

Structure:

## Короткое определение
Coverage = измерение того, какие части кода реально исполнились при прогоне тестов. Not a property of code but of code+tests+build+run. Analogy: маршрут обхода здания.

## Как измеряют механически
- basic blocks / edges; counters; instrumentation.
- два способа: статическое (компилятор вставляет счётчики: gcov, --coverage) и динамическое (инструментирование на лету, MSVC). Difference: no recompilation, works on optimized binaries, but needs the collector to launch/attach.
- MSVC tool exists on their machine (verified path), commands collect/merge/snapshot, formats coverage/xml/cobertura, -if include filter.
- why separate build/config: reproducibility; and on GCC coverage is compile-time; on MSVC dynamic → can use Release-like /O2 /Ob1 but still separate build tree is cleaner.
- report: per line/block, aggregates.

## Что считают: метрики
Table: function / line / block(branch proxy) / condition; hits; diff coverage. Explain what each catches and their project relevance. Note MSVC reports lines+blocks (block ~ basic block), partial line = some branch untaken. Confidence medium-high; verify in report.

## Что coverage НЕ говорит (critical)
- executed ≠ проверено (assert). A test that runs main and ignores output gives 100% lines and 0 value.
- 100% ≠ correctness / requirements. Missing feature not in code isn't counted.
- dead code can be uncovered forever or covered by dead tests.
- macros/inlining/templates distort mapping; /Ob1 mitigates; optimization can attribute lines weirdly.
- not for memory/races/perf (ASan/TSan/profiler).
- coverage of tests/infra isn't product coverage.
- Goodhart: target 80% invites gaming. Use as gap finder.
- branch coverage can't see condition combinations; for `a || b` you need both operands independently.

## Зачем в курсе и почему сейчас
- testbed complete before optimization (quote principle).
- mechanizes "код на доверии" — recall their own journal cases where manual audit found uncovered branches (t1 spaces/NUMBER_EMPTY, t1_low unused data, t3_x_y_z_k4, N=20, t2 multiword name). Coverage would have listed them.
- error paths ≥ happy path (course).
- before refactoring/optimization you want a quantified baseline; after changes, compare (but coverage is not a regression test by itself — tests are).
- the report is also a review artifact for mentor: numbers + list of uncovered branches with reason.

## Что такое покрытие — коротко

**Покрытие (code coverage) — это измерение того, какие части твоего кода реально исполнились во время прогона тестов.** Это не свойство кода самого по себе и не свойство тестов самих по себе: это свойство тройки «код + тесты + конкретная сборка + конкретный прогон». [ФАКТ, ВЫСОКИЙ]

Аналогия: у тебя есть здание с комнатами (строки/ветки кода) и обходчик с планом (тесты). Покрытие — это отметки на плане «в этой комнате был, в этой не был». Оно **не** говорит, что обходчик в комнате что-то проверил: он мог зайти, посмотреть в окно и уйти. Об этом — ниже, это главная ловушка метрики.

## Как это измеряется механически

Инструмент размечает машинный код на **basic blocks** — линейные участки без ветвлений внутри (условный переход только на границе блока). В каждый блок/ребро вставляется счётчик. После прогона счётчики агрегируются: строка считается покрытой, если исполнен хотя бы один её блок; **частично покрытой** — если исполнены не все блоки этой строки (то есть какая-то ветка на этой строке не сработала). [ФАКТ, ВЫСОКИЙ]

Два принципиально разных способа инструментирования:

| | Статическое | Динамическое |
|---|---|---|
| Кто вставляет счётчики | компилятор на этапе сборки | инструмент в момент запуска процесса |
| Пример | GCC/Clang `--coverage` → `.gcno`/`.gcda` | `Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console collect` |
| Нужна отдельная сборка | да | нет (можно гонять оптимизированный бинарь) |
| Точность при оптимизациях | страдает от инлайнинга | тоже страдает, поэтому рекомендуют ограничивать инлайнинг |

[ФАКТ, ВЫСОКИЙ по механике; конкретные рекомендации MSVC — сверяй с MS Learn]

## Что именно считают: метрики

| Метрика | На вопрос отвечает | Слабость |
|---|---|---|
| Function | «хоть одна функция модуля вызывалась?» | слишком грубо, почти всегда 100% |
| Line | «эта строка исполнялась?» | строка с `if` может быть «частично покрыта» |
| Block / branch | «обе стороны `if`/`else`/`switch` сработали?» | в MSVC это блоки, не «настоящие» ветки; смотри колонки отчёта |
| Condition | «каждый операнд `&&`/`\|\|` проверен отдельно?» | в MSVC-отчёте как отдельная метрика обычно нет |
| Hits (кратность) | «сколькими разными тестами покрыта строка?» | строка, покрытая одним тестом, — хрупкая |
| Diff-coverage | «покрыты ли только изменённые строки?» | имеет смысл при PR-процессе, которого у тебя пока нет |

Для твоего проекта самое ценное — **line + block + список непокрытых веток**, а не одно число. Число «80%» по всему репозиторию легко получается при 0% в отдельном модуле. [МНЕНИЕ, ВЫСОКИЙ]

## Что покрытие **не** говорит (критически важно)

1. **«Исполнено» ≠ «проверено».** Тест, который запускает `main.exe`, но не смотрит ни на stdout, ни на stderr, ни на код возврата, даст высокое покрытие и ноль пользы. Твоя текущая обвязка как раз проверяет три канала — это то, что делает покрытие осмысленным. [ФАКТ, ВЫСОКИЙ]
2. **100% ≠ корректность.** Покрытие не знает про требования. Фичи, которой нет в коде, в знаменателе тоже нет. Строка может быть покрыта и при этом считать `x + 1` вместо `x - 1`.
3. **Непокрытая строка не всегда дефект.** Может быть защитный `if (ptr == nullptr)` для недостижимого случая, платформенная ветка `#ifdef _WIN32`, или мёртвый код. Реакция бывает трёх видов: добавить тест, удалить код, задокументировать «недостижимо, потому что …». Третий вариант — самый частый соблазн соврать.
4. **Макросы, шаблоны, инлайнинг искажают привязку строк к бинарю.** Поэтому в курсе и написано: на GCC coverage не гонять выше `-O1`, а у MSVC рекомендация `/O2 /Ob1`. [ФАКТ по курсу, § 2.1.D]
5. **Покрытие — не замена ASan/TSan/профайлеру.** Оно не ловит use-after-free, гонки и не меряет время. У тебя ASan-сборка Debug — это отдельная ось, и с coverage она **не совмещается** (§ 2.1.D). [ФАКТ, ВЫСОКИЙ]
6. **Закон Гудхарта.** Как только «80%» становится KPI, появляются тесты без ассертов и вызовы функций «чтобы покрылось». Метрика должна работать как **поисковик дыр**, а не как оценка качества. [МНЕНИЕ, ВЫСОКИЙ]
7. **Покрытие тестовой обвязки — не покрытие продукта.** Если в знаменатель попадут gtest, boost, `e2e_runner`, сгенерированный `version.h` и vcpkg, число станет бессмысленным.

## Зачем это в курсе и почему именно сейчас

- По принципу из § 2.1.0: **testbed собирается полностью до оптимизаций**. Coverage — последний кусок этой инфраструктуры. Смысл: к моменту, когда ты начнёшь менять алгоритмы и параллелить, у тебя есть инструмент «что я вообще проверяю», а не два незнакомых инструмента одновременно. [ФАКТ по курсу]
- Coverage **механизирует то, что ты до сих пор делала руками**. В журнале это буквально повторяется: находились ветки «на доверии» — пустой ввод из одних пробелов в t1, неиспользованные `t1_low`/`t3_x_y_z_k4`, отсутствие теста на `N = 20`, имя фигуры из нескольких слов, ветка `NUMBER_EMPTY`. Каждый раз это обнаруживалось вопросом «где ещё?» и глазами. Отчёт даёт тот же список автоматически. [ФАКТ по твоему журналу]
- Требование курса: **покрытие error path не ниже happy path**, включая `if (!result)`-ветки (§ 2.1.0/03-ocenka). У тебя очень много веток — коды 64/65/66/74, «слишком много координат», «не-конечное число», help/version, неизвестный аргумент. Именно они — главный кандидат в отчёт.
- На контрольной точке это ещё и **артефакт для наставника**: не «я старалась», а «вот модуль, вот 12 непокрытых строк, вот по каждой причина — тест/удаление/недостижимо».

## Архитектурные оси, которые надо назвать **до** любых правок

Это ровно тот случай из § 4.2, где нельзя начинать с «запусти команду»:

1. **Знаменатель.** Что считаем продуктом: `common/*` + восемь `main.*`? Или только `common/`? Исключаем ли `tests/`, `sandbox/`, `gen_cloud/`, `hello/`, `build/`, `vcpkg_installed/`? Без ответа любое число бессмысленно.
2. **Конфигурация сборки.** У тебя Debug+ASan и Release. Coverage — **третья** сборка, не «переключатель»: ASan и coverage не смешиваются, а `/Ob1` отличается от release-дефолта. Либо отдельный `build/coverage` + пресет, либо явное решение переиспользовать Release с фиксацией, что тогда меряешь не то, что поставляешь.
3. **Дублирование модулей.** `common` компилируется в статическую библиотеку для t1–t2 и в shared — для t3–t4. Один и тот же исходник будет фигурировать несколькими модулями; агрегировать нужно **по файлу исходника**, иначе получишь либо двойной счёт, либо «0%», потому что смотрел не ту копию.
4. **Дерево процессов.** Это главный технический риск. `ctest` запускает gtest-исполняемые, а те уже через `boost::process` запускают `main.exe`. Соберёт ли `collect` покрытие **внуков**, а не только прямого ребёнка — я не знаю. [ПРЕДПОЛОЖЕНИЕ, НИЗКИЙ] Проверять надо пробой, как ты делала `bp_probe`, а не верить. Запасной путь есть: `instrument`/`uninstrument` (статические команды в том же инструменте) + обычный прогон + `merge`. Но инструментировать можно только копии бинарей — иначе испортишь артефакты сборки.
5. **Платформенная асимметрия.** io-fail тесты у тебя только под Linux (README, «известные ограничения»). На Windows эти ветки честно покажутся непокрытыми — это не дефект кода и не повод удалять ветку. Отчёт надо читать с этой поправкой.
6. **Куда класть отчёты.** `build/coverage/...` под `.gitignore`, формат — Cobertura (`-f cobertura` подтверждён в `--help`), потому что он переносим в CI/SonarQube. В репозиторий — только человеческое резюме и принятые решения, не сами отчёты.
7. **Одна точка входа** (§ 4.9 п.1). В итоге должна быть одна команда «собрать coverage-конфиг → прогнать suite под сборщиком покрытия → смержить → отдать Cobertura». Иначе появятся ручные последовательности, которые разойдутся.
8. **Семантика цели.** «80% глобально» vs «80% по каждому ключевому модулю + 100% достижимых error-веток». Второе честнее, но требует ручного разбора. Решать тебе.

## Микро-практика на понимание (не шаги слоя)

1. **Предсказание до измерения.** Возьми `common/string_utils.c` (`parse_int32`) и `t1_dist_matrix_c/main.c`. Выпиши: какие ветки существуют, каким конкретным кейсом из `t1_cases.hpp`/юнит-тестов покрывается каждая, и какие, по твоему мнению, **не покрыты**. Это фальсифицируемое предсказание — потом сверишь с отчётом. Ценность в расхождении: если ожидала «покрыто», а отчёт говорит «нет» — ты не понимала, какой тест что исполняет.
2. **Branch vs condition.** Для условия `N < MIN_SIZE || N > MAX_SIZE`: сколько прогонов нужно, чтобы покрыть обе ветки `if`, и сколько — чтобы проверить **каждый операнд** независимо? Какие из твоих кейсов (`t1_low`, `t1_high`, `N = 3`, `N = 20`) что дают? Это ровно та разница, из-за которой «ветки покрыты» и «логика проверена» — не одно и то же.
3. **Тест без ассертов.** Представь тест: запустить t1 с `N = 5`, ничего не проверить. Почему его вклад в line coverage может быть 90%, а в качество — ноль? Сформулируй одним предложением, что должно быть в тесте, чтобы покрытие строки что-то значило.

Then their suggested partition: [if] [n<3] [||] [n>20] [return data] — that's lexical tokens, not basic blocks. Basic blocks are maximal straight-line sequences of *instructions* with control flow entering only at the start and leaving only at the end. For the example:

```c
if (n < 3 || n > 20)
    return data;
```

Semantics: evaluate n<3; if true → body (return data); if false → evaluate n>20; if true → body; if false → fall through after if.

Basic blocks (conceptually, at source level):
- B1: evaluate `n < 3`; conditional branch to B3 if true, else B2.
- B2: evaluate `n > 20`; conditional branch to B3 if true, else B4.
- B3: `return data;` (then exit/unreachable after).
- B4: continue after the if.

Note: `||` is not a block—it's an operator that becomes a branch (short-circuit). `if` is not a block—it's control structure that creates the branch at the end of B1. `return data` is a block (or part of B3). And B4 exists even though not written — the fall-through path.

Also whether the function call/return creates edges: yes, `return` ends the block (term instruction). The `if` condition itself is not a "block" separate from comparison—the comparison instructions and the conditional jump are in one basic block.

How source lines map:
- line 1 `if (n < 3 || n > 20)` contains instructions of B1 and B2 → 2+ blocks per line.
- line 2 `return data;` → B3.
- B4 (fall-through) may map to line 1 or to the next statement's line.

The user asks: "то есть lines входят в blocks и блоки 'шире' строк? а не строки вложены в блоки"

Answer briefly. The truth: neither is a clean containment. Lines and blocks are two different partitions/views over the same instructions. A block can contain instructions from multiple lines (e.g., inlining, macro, or `if` condition and body on same line? Actually if body on same line, both blocks map to one line). A line can contain multiple blocks. So both directions of overlap exist; no nesting.

Best way: instructions are the atoms. Each instruction has (a) a block id and (b) a file:line. Both are many-to-many mappings. Not hierarchy.

Examples:
- Line 1 with `if (a || b)` → 2 blocks on one line: line → multiple blocks.
- `for (int i=0; i<n; ++i) { sum += i; }` written on one line → many blocks on one line.
- A single block can span multiple lines: `x = a + b;\ny = c + d;` straight-line code, no branches → one block, two lines (maybe more). So block → multiple lines.
- Macro/inlining → one line's code in many blocks across the binary.

So: "lines входят в blocks" is wrong as containment; "blocks шире строк" is wrong too. They're orthogonal labels on the same instructions. Only in the sense "a line typically maps to ≥1 block" and "a block typically maps to ≥1 line" — overlapping.

If forced to use containment: instructions ⊂ blocks, and instructions are attributed to lines. So both line and block are sets of instructions; these sets intersect, neither contains the other in general. Formally: intersection non-empty, difference in both directions possible.

Concretely: can a block contain only part of a line? Yes — `if (cond) foo();` all on one line: condition block and body block each are subsets of that line. Can a line contain partial block? Yes? Line partition cuts through a block: `int a = 1, b = 2;` on one line — one block; split by line? A block spanning lines 5-7: line 6 contains part of that block. So line contains part of a block → not containment either way.

Answer: no nesting; two independent partitions of the instruction stream; report is a projection.

The user asks: are they right that tests should use values to cover all branches? And why cover all branches — to understand all possible behaviors? Answer briefly, critically, with nuance.

They're partly right, but need nuance:
1. Yes, branch coverage is a reasonable test design heuristic.
2. But "cover all branches" is not the goal itself — the goal is verifying behavior at boundaries/error paths. Coverage finds gaps, not defines tests.
3. Some branches are equivalent/unreachable/defensive — can't or shouldn't be covered.
4. Each branch should be covered by a test with meaningful assertions, not just execution.
5. Choose values not at random: boundary values (3, 20, 2, 21), equivalence classes, error paths.
6. Covering all branches isn't the same as covering all "behaviors": state combinations, sequences, data-dependent logic. E.g., for t3 bbox, branch coverage doesn't test numeric correctness; output checks do.
7. Cost: combinatorial explosion for conditions; MC/DC etc.
8. In their project: error paths are a big part, and course requires coverage error path ≥ happy path.

Also connect: "чтобы понимать все возможные поведения" — yes, in the sense "all control-flow outcomes", but not all behaviors. Branch coverage is about control flow, not data. A branch can take both directions but the arithmetic can still be wrong. So tests must assert results.

Also, do they need to cover *every* branch? Some defensive branches (e.g., malloc failure) can't be triggered easily; you either inject faults or document. Their t4 has `if (!tmp)` after malloc — hard to test without fault injection. Coverage report will show it; the answer is not "force it" but "decide: fault injection, or documented unreachable-in-tests". Good concrete example from their code.

Also note: the goal isn't a number but "each branch has a reason to exist or is deleted". If a branch is unreachable, dead code → remove.

Also: "tests should have such values" — yes, but don't design tests by reading implementation only; risk of tests mirroring code. Better: derive from spec + boundaries, then use coverage to find what spec-driven tests missed. That's an important critical point (avoid implementation-coupled tests). Their e2e cases are spec-driven (input files + expected outputs); coverage report then reveals gaps.

Point 2: Yes, instructions are the smallest units. A basic block consists of instructions (machine instructions; at source level, roughly operations). Blocks are not atoms; instructions are. The hierarchy: instructions ⊂ basic block (as a set, plus edges between blocks). Note: block is a set of instructions with one entry and one exit; it's a maximal straight-line sequence.

Also note: "instruction" is binary-level; source statements don't map 1:1 to instructions. One source statement can compile to several instructions, and one instruction can be attributed to a line. The atom for coverage counting is the block (counters are per-block/edge), not the instruction, because instrumenting every instruction is expensive. So: physically smallest = instruction; accounting unit = block.

"Projection" explanation: The coverage tool records counters on blocks (B1 hit 5 times, B2 hit 0...). The report needs per-source-line view. For each line, it takes the set of blocks whose instructions are attributed (via debug line table) to that line, and aggregates: if any block hit > 0 → line hit; if all blocks hit > 0 → fully covered; if some 0 → partial. That aggregation is the "projection" — a many-to-one mapping from blocks to lines, losing information about which block specifically, unless the report shows blocks too. It's called projection because you collapse a richer structure (CFG with counters) onto a coarser label (line), discarding edges/order.

Analogy: like a heat map of a building projected onto a floor plan by room number: you have sensor readings per corridor segment (blocks), and you paint rooms (lines) based on which segments belong to which room; a room gets "visited" if any segment was visited, "fully visited" if all were. The map loses the path and order.

The user asks: inline hurts instrumentation because the final binary differs strongly from source and it's hard to understand which line/block it is?

Need to answer briefly with nuance. Plan mode read-only. No tools needed.

Answer: partly right, but precise mechanism matters. Inlining doesn't "make binary differ from source" in a general sense—it's that multiple source lines/functions collapse into one code region, and the debug line table attribution becomes ambiguous/approximate. Consequences:

1. A block may contain code from several source lines (inlined callee body) — one block maps to multiple lines, or the line table marks the call site instead of the callee.
2. A line may be attributed partially to the call site, so coverage of an inlined function may show as uncovered/partially covered even though it executed — or vice versa.
3. Blocks can disappear entirely (code folded, optimized away), so "uncovered block" may not exist in the binary.
4. Loops unrolled → one source line maps to many blocks; counters per unrolled copy aggregate, hiding which iteration/path.
5. Common subexpression elimination / code motion can attribute instructions to surprising lines, giving misleading hits.
6. Inlining across translation units / link-time codegen (LTCG) can merge identical functions (COMDAT folding, /OPT:ICF) — two source functions become one block; coverage can't distinguish them.

So it's not "binary differs → hard to know what block is", but "mapping instruction→line becomes many-to-many and lossy, and some blocks no longer correspond to the source structure you expect". Tools mitigate with /Ob1 (limits inlining) and by using debug line tables; still approximate.

Also note: this is why coverage is a diagnostic, not a precise proof; and why course says don't run coverage above -O1 on GCC, and MSVC recommends /O2 /Ob1.

Also mention: the report may show "partially covered" not because a branch wasn't taken, but because of inlining attribution artifacts. Need to verify by looking at assembly/debug info when in doubt.

Answer: It depends on the test. In their e2e tests, yes — `expect_case_matches` asserts exit code, primary channel content, and empty reverse channel. In unit tests, yes — EXPECT_EQ on returned value/error code. But coverage itself doesn't guarantee assertions; it merely executes. If someone adds a test case to the matrix and forgets expected output, the harness still asserts (it compares against the expected field; if empty string, it asserts emptiness). So the harness enforces a comparison for every case. But there are cases where coverage is collected while running e2e: every e2e test does assert. However, coverage collection could also include indirect code execution (e.g., help/version, destructors) that is asserted too.

Nuance: an assertion can be weak — EXPECT_EQ on something trivial, or the expected value itself wrong. So "assert exists" ≠ "assert meaningful". Also, e2e harness checks all three channels, so every e2e case has assertions by construction. In unit tests, each TEST_P has ASSERT/EXPECT.

Also: coverage doesn't check assertions; it just records execution. The guarantee comes from the test code, not from the coverage tool. If a path is only executed as a side effect of another test (e.g., version printing before input), the assertion tied to that test may not cover that path's output. Example: `handle_version_flag` runs in every test, but only version tests assert its output. Other tests assert different things; the version branch execution is incidental. Coverage would count it as covered, but its behavior isn't verified in those runs. This is a subtle and important point: "incidentally covered" code is not necessarily verified.

So answer:
1. In your current suite, yes: e2e `expect_case_matches` asserts code + primary channel + reverse channel emptiness; unit tests assert return value/error.
2. But coverage tool doesn't add assertions; it only records. If a new case is added with wrong/empty expected, the assertion exists but may be weak.
3. Paths executed incidentally (e.g., `--version` check at program start, cleanup/free paths, destructors) are "covered" but not necessarily asserted in that test. Coverage can't distinguish. So "covered" means executed, not verified — even in your suite.
4. Practical rule: when reading a coverage report, for each newly-covered branch ask "which test asserts the observable result of this branch?" If none, it's incidental coverage.

# делается до project, иначе будет падение не от моей проверки с моим сообщением,

# надо понять: "вложена" ли требуемая версия в имеющийся инстанс vcpkg. для этого используем git
# проверка что он есть - иначе нет инструмента для проверки
find_program(GIT_EXECUTABLE NAMES git)

  message(FATAL_ERROR "git was not found in PATH; it is required to check the vcpkg baseline")
endif()

# _vcpkg_manifest - весь vcpkg.json; _m - builtin-baseline найденный по regex  
file(READ "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/vcpkg.json" _vcpkg_manifest)
string(REGEX MATCH "\"builtin-baseline\"[ \t]*:[ \t]*\"([0-9a-fA-F]+)\"" _m "${_vcpkg_manifest}")
# если builtin-baseline не нашёлся, то падение с ошибкой

  set(CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Debug CACHE STRING "Build type (Debug/Release)" FORCE)
endif()
# переменная CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE уйдёт в кэш 
# кэш: для CMake, хранить инф. м-у выполнениями, и пользователь не повторяет ввод каждый раз
# FORCE вызовет перезапись параметра


# === ИСПРАВЛЕНИЕ DEFAULT-ФЛАГОВ ===
# CMAke дефолтно положит /RTC1 в debug-ветку. /RTC1 ловит ошибки в runtime, для этого лезет в стек и размечает его
# ASan - та же ф-ция. если оба будут менять стек, они помешают друг другу -> несовместимы. /RTC1 убирается 
# /incremental также несовместим с asan (именно по документации. так работало и когда оба вместе)
if(MSVC)
  string(REPLACE "/RTC1" "" CMAKE_C_FLAGS_DEBUG   "${CMAKE_C_FLAGS_DEBUG}")

endif()


# === ПОСТРОИТЬ КОМАНДЫ КОМПИЛЯЦИИ И ЛИНКА ===
function(configure_target trgt DBG)
if(MSVC)
  # минимальная поддерживаемая ОС - win7 (и все дальнейшие)
  target_compile_definitions(${trgt} PRIVATE _WIN32_WINNT=0x0601)
  # в msvc /Zi, /EHsc, /DEBUG  будут дублироваться, но прописываются для ясности
  # target_compile_options - произвольные флаги компилятора 
  # PRIVATE даёт нетранзитивность: А (этот объект) и Б к нему сможет линковаться. а когда К линк. к Б, то К не будет линк. к А
  target_compile_options(${trgt} PRIVATE $<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:/EHsc> /W4 /permissive-)

  # сюда будет заходить только для программ из задач, не для программ для тестирования (run_case, check) - им эти флаги не нужны
  if(DBG)
    # CMake проставит след. флаги автоматиечки: /Od /O2; /MDd /MD; /DNDEBUG
    target_compile_options(${trgt} PRIVATE $<$<CONFIG:Debug>:/Zi /fsanitize=address> $<$<CONFIG:Release>:/Zi>)
    target_link_options(${trgt} PRIVATE $<$<CONFIG:Debug>:/DEBUG> $<$<CONFIG:Release>:/DEBUG /OPT:REF /OPT:ICF>)
  endif()

else()
  target_compile_options(${trgt} PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra)
  # и в ветке продуктов, и в ветке тестовых программ оптимизация на релизе будет именно -O2, а не cmake-default -O3
  if (DBG) 
    # -O0 на дебаге будет подтянут CMake автоматически, а на релизе -DNDEBUG
    target_compile_options(${trgt} PRIVATE $<$<CONFIG:Debug>: -g -fsanitize=address> $<$<CONFIG:Release>: -g -O2>)
    target_link_options(${trgt} PRIVATE $<$<CONFIG:Debug>: -fsanitize=address>)
  else()
    target_compile_options(${trgt} PRIVATE $<$<CONFIG:Release>: -O2>)
  endif()
endif()
endfunction()


# === Ф-ЦИЯ ДОБАВЛЕНИЯ ЗАДАЧИ === 
# сборки exe из main.c/main.cpp; уходит в каталог build/cfg/dir
function(add_task dir trgt src lib)
  # добавление исполняемного файла 
  # цель и её исходник. цель имеет одно имя (логическое, типа t1_c), а сделанный ею файл - другое (OUTPUT_NAME main)
  add_executable(${trgt} ${src})

  # в CMAKE_BINARY_DIR будет тот каталог, который был передан по -B
  set_target_properties(${trgt} PROPERTIES
  OUTPUT_NAME main
  RUNTIME_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/${dir})

  # с кем линкуемся
  # тут private не имеет смысла (.exe конечен, к нему не линкуются), просто для единообразия
  target_link_libraries(${trgt} PRIVATE ${lib})

  # определение типа библиотеки т.к. на windows для .dll нужно доп. действие для связки с .exe
  get_target_property(lib_type ${lib} TYPE)
  # копирование dll в папку к exe даже если сам exe не перестраивался
  if(WIN32 AND lib_type STREQUAL "SHARED_LIBRARY")
    set(copied_dll "${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/${dir}/${lib}.dll")
    add_custom_command(OUTPUT "${copied_dll}"
      COMMAND ${CMAKE_COMMAND} -E copy_if_different $<TARGET_FILE:${lib}> "${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}/${dir}"
      DEPENDS ${lib} 
      COMMENT "Copying DLL ${lib} next to ${trgt}"
      VERBATIM)
    add_custom_target(${trgt}_dll DEPENDS "${copied_dll}")
    add_dependencies(${trgt} ${trgt}_dll)
  endif()

  # команда для cl+link. флаг DEBUG = ON - т.е. пойдём по ветке if (DBG) с флагами для программ-задач
  configure_target(${trgt} ON)
 
endfunction()

# cmake/format.cmake в скриптовом режиме. отделен он графа сборки проекта
set(FORMAT_SCRIPT "${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/cmake/format.cmake")

# исключаем весь каталог сборки, а не только текущую конфигурацию:
# конфигурации вложены (build/debug, build/release)

Now I understand the build. Key facts:
- `configure_target(trgt DBG)` uses generator expressions `$<$<CONFIG:Debug>:...>` and `$<$<CONFIG:Release>:...>`. A custom `Coverage` config would not match either, so it would get no `/Zi`, no `/DEBUG`, no ASan (good) but also no debug info and no `/O2` explicit (CMake would apply `CMAKE_C_FLAGS_COVERAGE` if defined; default empty). Need to add Coverage branches.
- CMake build type "Coverage" is not one of the default configs; CMake allows arbitrary `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE`, but `CMAKE_C_FLAGS_COVERAGE` must be set. Also CMake may not define `NDEBUG`; only Release/RelWithDebInfo/MinSizeRel get `-DNDEBUG`. For coverage we might want NDEBUG or not. Not critical.
- Tests use `configure_target(target OFF)` → no `/Zi`/ASan; on Release, no `-O2` for MSVC tests (CMake default `/O2`? Actually CMake's default Release flags include `/O2 /DNDEBUG`; `configure_target` for MSVC tests adds nothing config-specific, so CMake's defaults apply: Debug `/Od /Zi`, Release `/O2 /DNDEBUG`). For Coverage config, CMake default flags would be empty unless we define them. Fine—tests can be built with default (no optimization, no debug info? On MSVC default CFLAGS has `/Zi`? CMake default MSVC flags include `/Zi` for Debug, and for other configs maybe `/O2`? Need not worry).
- `add_task` copies shared DLL next to exe via custom target; fine.
- The version header generated per build dir.
- Tests: `gtest_discover_tests` at build time; e2e exes are in `build/<cfg>/tests/e2e/`, products in `build/<cfg>/tN_.../main.exe`.
- `e2e_runner` opens input/output files itself and passes FILE* to boost::process; so products get stdin from a file, stdout/stderr to files. Coverage collector must follow: ctest → t1_e2e.exe → main.exe. The e2e exe is launched by ctest; main.exe by boost::process (CreateProcess). The collector must instrument descendants.
- Unit test exes also link common libs directly; they run common code, good for coverage of common.
- There are 4 e2e exes + 1 runner test + many unit exes. Under coverage, all get instrumented, but filter output to product.

- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/test/microsoft-code-coverage-console-tool?view=vs-2022
Maybe for VS 2026 `view=vs-2026`? Let's try 2022; content likely similar. Use webfetch.

Also maybe docs on `--settings` XML and include/exclude. Let's fetch.

# Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console tool - Visual Studio (Windows) | Microsoft Learn

Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console is a command-line tool that you can use to collect code coverage for C++ and C# code. It also supports merging and converting code coverage reports. This tool can be used to collect code coverage in non-test scenarios (for example, for a simple console application).

This tool is an extension to the [dotnet-coverage](/en-us/dotnet/core/additional-tools/dotnet-coverage) dotnet tool that adds support for the following scenarios:

- Adds security features to enable collecting ASP.NET code coverage data from IIS.
- Collecting code coverage for C++ code.

::: moniker range="visualstudio"

Note

Code coverage is available in Visual Studio Enterprise, Community, and Professional editions. In Visual Studio 2022 and previous versions, the code coverage feature was limited to Visual Studio Enterprise edition.

::: moniker-end

::: moniker range="vs-2022"

Note

Code coverage is available only with Visual Studio Enterprise. For .NET code coverage, you can alternatively use the command-line tool, [dotnet-coverage](/en-us/dotnet/core/additional-tools/dotnet-coverage).

::: moniker-end

Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console is available in Visual Studio 2022 17.3 under the folder `Common7\IDE\Extensions\Microsoft\CodeCoverage.Console`. You can use it in a Developer Command Prompt and a Developer PowerShell:

```console
D:\ConsoleApplication\x64\Debug>Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console --help

Description:
  Code coverage tools.

Usage:
  Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console [command] [options]

Options:
  --version       Show version information
  -?, -h, --help  Show help and usage information

Commands:
  collect <command> <args>            Collect code coverage from inner process and subprocesses.
  connect <session> <command> <args>  Connects to an existing code coverage session and collects code coverage from
                                      inner process and subprocesses.
  merge <files>                       Merge coverage reports
  shutdown <session>                  Close existing code coverage collection.
  snapshot <session>                  Creates coverage file for existing code coverage collection.
  instrument <input-file>             Instruments native and managed binary.
  uninstrument <input-file>           Restore original binary.
```

## Collect, connect, shutdown, merge, snapshot, and uninstrument commands

The Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console tool is an extension to the [dotnet-coverage](/en-us/dotnet/core/additional-tools/dotnet-coverage) dotnet tool. The documentation for collect, connect, shutdown, merge, snapshot, and uninstrument commands can be found [here](/en-us/dotnet/core/additional-tools/dotnet-coverage).

Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console supports additional security features to enable collecting ASP.NET code coverage data from IIS. Additionally, the Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console tool supports collecting code coverage for C++ code. The `instrument` command is specific to these scenarios.

## Instrument command

The instrument command is used to instrument native or managed binary on disk.

### Synopsis

```console
Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console instrument
    <input-file>
    [-s|--settings <settings>] [-id|--session-id <session-id>]
    [-o|--output <output>]
    [-l|--log-file <log-file>] [-ll|--log-level <log-level>]
    [-dco|--disable-console-output] [--nologo]
    [-?|-h|--help]
```

### Arguments

- **`<input-file>`**

    The input binary.

### Options

- **`-s|--settings <settings>`**

    Sets the path to the XML code coverage settings. The settings file can be used to exclude some modules or methods from code coverage analysis. The format is the same as the data collector configuration inside a *.runsettings* file. For more information, see [Customize code coverage analysis](customizing-code-coverage-analysis).
- **`-id|--session-id <session-id>`**

    Specifies the code coverage session ID. If not provided, the tool generates a random GUID.
- **`-o|--output <output>`**

    Sets the path to output file binary. If not provided, instrumentation will be performed in-place.
- **`-l|--log-file <log-file>`**

    Sets the log file path. When you provide a directory (with a path separator at the end), a new log file is generated for each process under analysis.
- **`-ll|--log-level <log-level>`**

    Sets the log level. Supported values: `Error`, `Info`, and `Verbose`.
- **`-dco|--disable-console-output`**

    Disables console output.
- **`--nologo`**

    Do not display Code Coverage banner.

## Static code coverage for C++ code

The Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console tool can be used to collect code coverage for C++ using static instrumentation. There are three different methods available that you can use. To demonstrate, let's assume we have a simple C++ console application (linked with the option [/PROFILE](/en-us/cpp/build/reference/profile-performance-tools-profiler)):

```console
D:\ConsoleApplication\x64\Debug> .\ConsoleApplication.exe
Hello World!
```

### Code coverage using collect command with configuration file (C++)

If you don't want to use the `instrument` command, you can instead use a configuration file to specify the files to instrument, as follows:

```xml
<ModulePaths>
  <IncludeDirectories>
    <Directory>D:\ConsoleApplication\x64\Debug</Directory>
  </IncludeDirectories>
</ModulePaths>
```

Then, collect code coverage as follows:

```console
D:\ConsoleApplication\x64\Debug>Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console collect --settings coverage.config .\ConsoleApplication.exe
SessionId: 85d9d49e-38a7-43a4-81ff-9e12f0e6b04b
Hello World!
Code coverage results: output.coverage.
```

The settings file can be used to exclude some modules or methods from code coverage analysis. The format is the same as the data collector configuration inside a *.runsettings* file. For more information, see [Customize code coverage analysis](customizing-code-coverage-analysis).

### Code coverage using instrument and collect commands (C++)

Before collecting code coverage data, first instrument the binary as follows:

```console
D:\ConsoleApplication\x64\Debug>Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console instrument ConsoleApplication.exe
Input file successfully instrumented.
```

Then, collect code coverage as follows:

```console
D:\ConsoleApplication\x64\Debug>Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console collect .\ConsoleApplication.exe
SessionId: e85e657f-9ff3-42a0-88d7-2349598a1ecd
Hello World!
Code coverage results: output.coverage.
```

### Code coverage using instrument command and collect command in server mode (C++)

Using this method, you can separate code coverage collection from running your application. First, instrument your binary as follows:

```console
D:\ConsoleApplication\x64\Debug>Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console instrument --session-id 73c34ce5-501c-4369-a4cb-04d31427d1a4 ConsoleApplication.exe
Input file successfully instrumented.
```

Note

Session ID needs to be used in this scenario to make sure that the application can connect and provide data to external collector.

In the second step, you need to start the code coverage collector as follows:

```console
D:\ConsoleApplication\x64\Debug>Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console collect --session-id 73c34ce5-501c-4369-a4cb-04d31427d1a4 --server-mode
SessionId: 73c34ce5-501c-4369-a4cb-04d31427d1a4
```

Then, start the application as follows:

```console
D:\ConsoleApplication\x64\Debug>.\ConsoleApplication.exe
Hello World!
```

Note

Instrumented native binary contains a reference to `static_covrun64.dll`. Make sure that this file is next to the instrumented binary or the directory where `static_covrun64.dll` is located is listed in the `Path` environment variable. The `collect` and `connect` commands are adding proper directories to `Path` automatically.

Finally, close the collector as follows:

```console
D:\ConsoleApplication\x64\Debug>Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console shutdown 73c34ce5-501c-4369-a4cb-04d31427d1a4
```

# Customizing Code Coverage Analysis - Visual Studio (Windows) | Microsoft Learn

By default, code coverage analyzes all solution assemblies that are loaded during unit tests. We recommend that you use this default behavior, because it works well most of the time. For more information, see [Use code coverage to determine how much code is tested](using-code-coverage-to-determine-how-much-code-is-being-tested).

To exclude test code from the code coverage results and only include application code, add the [ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.diagnostics.codeanalysis.excludefromcodecoverageattribute) attribute to your test class.

To include assemblies that aren't part of your solution, obtain the *.pdb* files for these assemblies and copy them into the same folder as the assembly *.dll* files.

::: moniker range="visualstudio"

Note

Code coverage is available in Visual Studio Enterprise, Community, and Professional editions. In Visual Studio 2022 and previous versions, the code coverage feature was limited to Visual Studio Enterprise edition.

::: moniker-end

::: moniker range="vs-2022"

Note

Code coverage is available only with Visual Studio Enterprise. For .NET code coverage, you can alternatively use the command-line tool, [dotnet-coverage](/en-us/dotnet/core/additional-tools/dotnet-coverage).

::: moniker-end

## Run settings file

The [run settings file](configure-unit-tests-by-using-a-dot-runsettings-file) is the configuration file used by unit testing tools. Advanced code coverage settings are specified in a *.runsettings* file.

To customize code coverage, follow these steps:

1. Add a run settings file to your solution. In **Solution Explorer**, on the shortcut menu of your solution, choose **Add** > **New Item**, and select **XML File**. Save the file with a name such as *CodeCoverage.runsettings*.

    If you don't see all the item templates, choose **Show All Templates**, and then choose the item template.
2. Add the content from the example file at the end of this article, and then customize it to your needs as described in the sections that follow.
3. Select a run settings file.

::: moniker range="visualstudio vs-2022"

Starting in Visual Studio 2019 version 16.4, you can autodetect a run settings file in the project root. Otherwise, on the **Test** menu, choose **Configure Run Settings**, and then choose **Select Solution Wide runsettings File**. To specify a run settings file for running tests from the command line, see [Configure unit tests](configure-unit-tests-by-using-a-dot-runsettings-file#specify-a-run-settings-file-from-the-command-line).

When you select **Analyze Code Coverage**, the configuration information is read from the run settings file.

Tip

Any previous code coverage results and code coloring aren't automatically hidden when you run tests or update your code.

To turn the custom settings off and on, deselect or select the file on the **Test** menu.

::: moniker-end

## Symbol search paths

Code coverage requires symbol files (*.pdb* files) for assemblies. For assemblies built by your solution, symbol files are usually present alongside the binary files, and code coverage works automatically. In some cases, you might want to include referenced assemblies in your code coverage analysis. In such cases, the *.pdb* files might not be adjacent to the binaries, but you can specify the symbol search path in the *.runsettings* file.

```xml
<SymbolSearchPaths>
      <Path>\\mybuildshare\builds\ProjectX</Path>
      <!--More paths if required-->
</SymbolSearchPaths>
```

Note

Symbol resolution can take time, especially when using a remote file location with many assemblies. Therefore, consider copying *.pdb* files to the same local location as the binary (*.dll* and *.exe*) files.

## Include or exclude assemblies and members

You can include or exclude assemblies or specific types and members from code coverage analysis. If the **Include** section is empty or omitted, then all assemblies that are loaded and have associated PDB files are included. If an assembly or member matches a clause in the **Exclude** section, then it is excluded from code coverage. The **Exclude** section takes precedence over the **Include** section: if an assembly is listed in both **Include** and **Exclude**, it will not be included in code coverage.

For example, the following XML excludes a single assembly by specifying its name:

```xml
<ModulePaths>
  <Exclude>
   <ModulePath>.*Fabrikam.Math.UnitTest.dll</ModulePath>
   <!-- Add more ModulePath nodes here. -->
  </Exclude>
</ModulePaths>
```

The following example specifies that only a single assembly should be included in code coverage:

```xml
<ModulePaths>
  <Include>
   <ModulePath>.*Fabrikam.Math.dll</ModulePath>
   <!-- Add more ModulePath nodes here. -->
  </Include>
</ModulePaths>
```

The following table shows the various ways that assemblies and members can be matched for inclusion in or exclusion from code coverage.

| XML element | What it matches |
| --- | --- |
| ModulePath | Matches assemblies specified by assembly name or file path. |
| CompanyName | Matches assemblies by the **Company** attribute. |
| PublicKeyToken | Matches signed assemblies by the public key token. |
| Source | Matches elements by the path name of the source file in which they're defined. |
| Attribute | Matches elements that have the specified attribute. Specify the full name of the attribute, for example `<Attribute>^System\.Diagnostics\.DebuggerHiddenAttribute$</Attribute>`.If you exclude the [CompilerGeneratedAttribute](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.compilerservices.compilergeneratedattribute) attribute, code that uses language features such as `async`, `await`, `yield return`, and auto-implemented properties is excluded from code coverage analysis. To exclude truly generated code, only exclude the [GeneratedCodeAttribute](/en-us/dotnet/api/system.codedom.compiler.generatedcodeattribute) attribute. |
| Function | Matches procedures, functions, or methods by fully qualified name, including the parameter list. You can also match part of the name by using a regular expression.Examples:`Fabrikam.Math.LocalMath.SquareRoot(double);` (C#)`Fabrikam::Math::LocalMath::SquareRoot(double)` (C++) |

::: moniker range="visualstudio vs-2022"

### Code coverage formats

By default code coverage is collected and saved in a `.coverage` file. You can also collect coverage using other formats including XML and Cobertura. Different formats may be useful across different editors and pipelines. You can enable this in runsettings by adding `<Format>Cobertura</Format>` or `<Format>Xml</Format>` in the [DataCollector configuration section in your runsettings file](configure-unit-tests-by-using-a-dot-runsettings-file#codecoverage-data-collector). This format can be viewed in the code coverage results window in Visual Studio.

You can also specify different formats from the command-line by either specifying it in the runsettings file or specifying it in a parameter. For example, the dotnet command-line use `dotnet test --collect:"Code Coverage;Format=Cobertura"`. For vstest use `vstest.console.exe /collect:"Code Coverage;Format=Cobertura"`. The collect parameter will override the format specified in runsettings.

::: moniker-end

::: moniker range="visualstudio vs-2022"

### Static and dynamic native instrumentation

In Visual Studio 2022 version 17.2, we added the option to instrument native binary statically (on disk). In previous versions, we supported only dynamic instrumentation, which was often not able to instrument methods. Static native instrumentation is more stable and it is recommended. Static native instrumentation requires enabling the [/PROFILE](/en-us/cpp/build/reference/profile-performance-tools-profiler) link option for all native projects for which you need code coverage collection.

You can also enable native static instrumentation in runsettings by adding `<EnableStaticNativeInstrumentation>True</EnableStaticNativeInstrumentation>` under `<CodeCoverage>` tag. Use this method for command line scenarios.

By default, dynamic native instrumentation is always enabled. If both static and dynamic instrumentation is enabled, Visual Studio tries to instrument your C++ code statically, but if this is not possible (for example, when the `/PROFILE` link option is not enabled), dynamic instrumentation will be used. You can fully disable dynamic native instrumentation in runsettings by adding `<EnableDynamicNativeInstrumentation>False</EnableDynamicNativeInstrumentation>` under `<CodeCoverage>`.

When static native instrumentation is enabled, native binaries will be instrumented and replaced on disk before test execution. Original binaries will be restored after test execution. You can disable restoring original files in runsettings by adding `<EnableStaticNativeInstrumentationRestore>False</EnableStaticNativeInstrumentationRestore>` under the `<CodeCoverage>` tag. This can be especially useful in CI scenarios.

When static native instrumentation is enabled, Visual Studio will search and instrument all native binaries in directory where test binary is located. You can specify additional directories where binaries should be searched. The following example specifies that all native binaries from `C:\temp` and its subdirectories should be instrumented except files ending with `Fabrikam.Math.dll`.

```xml
<ModulePaths>
  <IncludeDirectories>
    <Directory Recursive="true">C:\temp</Directory>
  </IncludeDirectories>
  <Exclude>
    <ModulePath>.*Fabrikam.Math.dll</ModulePath>
  </Exclude>
</ModulePaths>
```

::: moniker-end

### Include or exclude test assemblies

To include or exclude test assemblies from the coverage report, you can use the `<IncludeTestAssembly>` element in the `<Configuration>` section of your .runsettings file.

In this example, setting `<IncludeTestAssembly>` to `False` will exclude test assemblies from the code coverage report. If you want to include test assemblies, set it to `True`.

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<!-- File name extension must be .runsettings -->
<RunSettings>
  <DataCollectionRunSettings>
    <DataCollectors>
      <DataCollector friendlyName="Code Coverage" uri="datacollector://Microsoft/CodeCoverage/2.0" assemblyQualifiedName="Microsoft.VisualStudio.Coverage.DynamicCoverageDataCollector, Microsoft.VisualStudio.TraceCollector, Version=11.0.0.0, Culture=neutral, PublicKeyToken=b03f5f7f11d50a3a">
        <Configuration>
          <IncludeTestAssembly>False</IncludeTestAssembly>
          ...
        </Configuration>
      </DataCollector>
    </DataCollectors>
  </DataCollectionRunSettings>
</RunSettings>
```

Note

The default value of `IncludeTestAssembly` in [VSTest](/en-us/visualstudio/test/vstest-console-options) is `true`, while it is `false` in [Microsoft.Testing.Platform](/en-us/dotnet/core/testing/microsoft-testing-platform-extensions-code-coverage). This means that test projects are included by default. For more information, see [Code Coverage configuration](https://github.com/microsoft/codecoverage/blob/main/docs/configuration.md).

### Regular expressions

Include and exclude nodes use regular expressions, which aren't the same as wildcards. All matches are case-insensitive. Some examples are:

- **.\*** matches a string of any characters
- **\.** matches a dot "."
- **\( \)** matches parentheses "( )"
- **\\** matches a file path delimiter "\"
- **^** matches the start of the string
- **$** matches the end of the string

The following XML shows how to include and exclude specific assemblies by using regular expressions:

```xml
<ModulePaths>
  <Include>
```

```console
dotnet-coverage <command> [-h, --help] [--version]
```

## Description

The `dotnet-coverage` tool:

- Enables the cross-platform collection of code coverage data of a running process.
- Provides cross-platform merging of code coverage reports.

## Options

- **`-h|--help`**

    Shows command-line help.
- **`--version`**

    Displays the version of the dotnet-coverage utility.

## Install

To install the latest release version of the `dotnet-coverage`[NuGet package](https://www.nuget.org/packages/dotnet-coverage), use the [dotnet tool install](../tools/dotnet-tool-install) command:

```dotnetcli
dotnet tool install --global dotnet-coverage
```

## Commands

| Command |
| --- |
| dotnet-coverage merge |
| dotnet-coverage collect |
| dotnet-coverage connect |
| dotnet-coverage snapshot |
| dotnet-coverage shutdown |
| dotnet-coverage instrument |
| dotnet-coverage uninstrument |

## dotnet-coverage merge

The `merge` command is used to merge several code coverage reports into one. This command is available on all platforms. This command supports the following code coverage report formats:

- `coverage`
- `cobertura`
- `xml`

### Synopsis

```console
dotnet-coverage merge
    <files>...
    [--remove-input-files]
    [-o|--output <output>] [-f|--output-format <output-format>]
    [-l|--log-file <log-file>] [-ll|--log-level <log-level>]
    [-dco|--disable-console-output] [--nologo]
    [-?|-h|--help]
```

### Arguments

- **`<files>`**

    The input code coverage reports.

### Options

- **`--remove-input-files`**

    Removes all input coverage reports that were merged.
- **`-r, --recursive`**

    .NET 7 SDK and earlier versions only Search for coverage reports in subdirectories.
- **`-o|--output <output>`**

    Sets the code coverage report output file.
- **`-f|--output-format <output-format>`**

    The output file format. Supported values: `coverage`, `xml`, and `cobertura`. Default is `coverage` (binary format that can be opened in Visual Studio).
- **`-l|--log-file <log-file>`**

    Sets the log file path. When you provide a directory (with a path separator at the end), a new log file is generated for each process under analysis.
- **`-ll|--log-level <log-level>`**

    Sets the log level. Supported values: `Error`, `Info`, and `Verbose`.
- **`-dco|--disable-console-output`**

    Disables console output.
- **`--nologo`**

    Do not display Code Coverage banner.

## dotnet-coverage collect

The `collect` command is used to collect code coverage data for any .NET process and its subprocesses. For example, you can collect code coverage data for a console application or a Blazor application. This command supports dynamic and static instrumentation. Static instrumentation is available on all platforms. You can specify files to be statically instrumented using `include-files` option. Dynamic instrumentation is available on Windows (x86, x64 and Arm64), Linux (x64), and macOS (x64). The command supports only .NET modules. Native modules are not supported.

### Synopsis

The `collect` command can run in two modes.

#### Command Mode

The `collect` command will collect code coverage for the given process executed by the `command` argument.

```console
dotnet-coverage collect
    <command> <args>...
    [-s|--settings <settings>] [-id|--session-id <session-id>]
    [-if|--include-files <include-files>] [-o|--output <output>] [-f|--output-format <output-format>]
    [-l|--log-file <log-file>] [-ll|--log-level <log-level>]
    [-dco|--disable-console-output] [--nologo]
    [-?|-h|--help]
```

#### Server Mode

The `collect` command hosts a server for code coverage collection. Clients can connect to the server via `connect` command.

```console
dotnet-coverage collect
    [-s|--settings <settings>] [-id|--session-id <session-id>]
    [-sv|--server-mode] [-b|--background] [-t|--timeout]
    [-if|--include-files <include-files>] [-o|--output <output>] [-f|--output-format <output-format>]
    [-l|--log-file <log-file>] [-ll|--log-level <log-level>]
    [-dco|--disable-console-output] [--nologo]
    [-?|-h|--help]
```

### Arguments

- **`<command>`**

    The command for which to collect code coverage data.
- **`<args>`**

    The command line arguments for the command.

### Options

- **`-s|--settings <settings>`**

    Sets the path to the XML code coverage settings.
- **`-id|--session-id <session-id>`**

    Specifies the code coverage session ID. If not provided, the tool will generate a random GUID.
- **`-sv|--server-mode`**

    Starts the collector in server mode. Clients can connect to the server with the `connect` command.
- **`-b|--background`**

    Starts code coverage collection server in a new background process. Clients can connect to the server with the `connect` command.
- **`-t|--timeout`**

    Timeout (in milliseconds) for interprocess communication between clients and the server.
- **`-if|--include-files <include-files>`**

    Specifies list of files to be statically instrumented.
- **`-o|--output <output>`**

    Sets the code coverage report output file.
- **`-f|--output-format <output-format>`**

    The output file format. Supported values: `coverage`, `xml`, and `cobertura`. Default is `coverage` (binary format that can be opened in Visual Studio).
- **`-l|--log-file <log-file>`**

    Sets the log file path. When you provide a directory (with a path separator at the end), a new log file is generated for each process under analysis.
- **`-ll|--log-level <log-level>`**

    Sets the log level. Supported values: `Error`, `Info`, and `Verbose`.
- **`-dco|--disable-console-output`**

    Disables console output.
- **`--nologo`**

    Do not display Code Coverage banner.

## dotnet-coverage connect

The `connect` command is used to connect with the existing server and collects code coverage data for any .NET process and its subprocesses. For example, you can collect code coverage data for a console application or a Blazor application. The command supports only .NET modules. Native modules are not supported.

Note

Command will use dynamic instrumentation for all subprocesses which is available on Windows (x86, x64 and Arm64), Linux (x64), and macOS (x64). If you need to statically instrument any .NET module use `instrument` command (with corresponding session ID option) before executing `connect` command.

### Synopsis

```console
dotnet-coverage connect
    <session> <command> <args>...
    [-b|--background] [-t|--timeout]
    [-l|--log-file <log-file>] [-ll|--log-level <log-level>]
    [-dco|--disable-console-output] [--nologo]
    [-?|-h|--help]
```

### Arguments

- **`<session>`**

    The session ID of the server hosted by the `collect` command.
- **`<command>`**

    The command for which to collect code coverage data.
- **`<args>`**

    The command line arguments for the command.

### Options

- **`-b|--background`**

    Starts the client in a new background process.
- **`-t|--timeout`**

    Timeout (in milliseconds) for interprocess communication between the client and the server.\* **`-l|--log-file <log-file>`**
- **`-l|--log-file <log-file>`**

    Sets the log file path. When you provide a directory (with a path separator at the end), a new log file is generated for each process under analysis.
- **`-ll|--log-level <log-level>`**

    Sets the log level. Supported values: `Error`, `Info`, and `Verbose`.
- **`-dco|--disable-console-output`**

    Disables console output.
- **`--nologo`**

    Do not display Code Coverage banner.

## dotnet-coverage snapshot

Creates a coverage file for existing code coverage collection.

### Synopsis

```console
dotnet-coverage snapshot
    <session>
    [-r|--reset]
    [-tn|--tag-name <tag-name>] [-tid|--tag-identifier <tag-identifier>]
    [-o|--output <output>]
    [-t|--timeout]
    [-l|--log-file <log-file>] [-ll|--log-level <log-level>]
```

### Arguments

### Options

- **`-r|--reset <reset>`**

    Clears existing coverage information after a coverage file is created.
- **`-tn|--tag-name <tag-name>`**

    Creates a snapshot tag name in the coverage file with current coverage information. Tag-name and tag-identifier are mutually inclusive.
- **`-tid|--tag-identifier <tag-identifier>`**

    Creates a snapshot tag identifier in the coverage file with current coverage information. Tag-name and tag-identifier are mutually inclusive.
- **`-o|--output <output>`**

    Sets the code coverage report output file. If not provided, it's generated automatically with a timestamp.
- **`-t|--timeout`**

    Timeout (in milliseconds) for interprocess communication between the client and the server.
- **`-l|--log-file <log-file>`**

    Sets the log file path. When you provide a directory (with a path separator at the end), a new log file is generated for each process under analysis.
- **`-ll|--log-level <log-level>`**

    Sets the log level. Supported values: `Error`, `Info`, and `Verbose`.
- **`-dco|--disable-console-output`**

    Disables console output.

## Sample scenarios

## Collecting code coverage

Collect code coverage data for any .NET application (such as console or Blazor) by using the following command:

```console
dotnet-coverage collect dotnet run
```

In case of an application that requires a signal to terminate, you can use Ctrl+C, which will still let you collect code coverage data. For the argument, you can provide any command that will eventually start a .NET app. For example, it can be a PowerShell script.

### Sessions

When you're running code coverage analysis on a .NET server that just waits for messages and sends responses, you need a way to stop the server to get final code coverage results. You can use Ctrl+C locally, but not in Azure Pipelines. For these scenarios, you can use sessions. You can specify a session ID when starting collection, and then use the `shutdown` command to stop collection and the server.

For example, assume you have a server in the *D:\serverexample\server* directory and a test project in the *D:\serverexample\tests* directory. Tests are communicating with the server through the network. You can start code coverage collection for the server as follows:

```console
D:\serverexample\server> dotnet-coverage collect --session-id serverdemo "dotnet run"
```

Session ID was specified as `serverdemo`. Then you can run tests as follows:

```console
D:\serverexample\tests> dotnet test
```

A code coverage file for session `serverdemo` can be generated with current coverage as follows:

```console
dotnet-coverage snapshot --output after_first_test.coverage serverdemo
```

Also, a snapshot tag can be added to the coverage file using tag options as follows:

```console
dotnet-coverage snapshot --tag-name after_first_test --tag-identifier after_first_test serverdemo
```

Finally, session `serverdemo` and the server can be closed as follows:

```console
dotnet-coverage shutdown serverdemo
```

Following is an example of full output on the server side:

```console
D:\serverexample\server> dotnet-coverage collect --session-id serverdemo "dotnet run"
SessionId: serverdemo
Waiting for a connection... Connected!
Received: Hello!
Sent: HELLO!
Waiting for a connection... Code coverage results: output.coverage.
D:\serverexample\server>
```

### Server and client mode

Code coverage collection can be done in server-client mode as well. In this scenario, a code coverage collection server starts, and multiple clients can connect with the server. Code coverage is collected for all the clients collectively.

Start the code coverage server using the following command:

```condole
dotnet-coverage collect --session-id serverdemo --server-mode
```

In this example, the session ID was specified as `serverdemo` for the server. A client can connect to the server using this session ID using the following command:

```condole
dotnet-coverage connect serverdemo dotnet run
```

Finally, you can close the session `serverdemo` and the server using the following command:

```console
dotnet-coverage shutdown serverdemo
```

The server process creates a collective code coverage report for all clients and exits.

Following is an example of full output on the server side:

```console
D:\serverexample\server> dotnet-coverage collect --session-id serverdemo --server-mode
SessionId: serverdemo
// Server will be in idle state and wait for connect and shutdown commands
Code coverage results: output.coverage.
D:\serverexample\server>
```

Following is an example of full output on the client side:

```console
D:\serverexample\server> dotnet-coverage connect serverdemo ConsoleApplication.exe World
Hello World!!
D:\serverexample\server> dotnet-coverage connect serverdemo WpfApplication.exe
D:\serverexample\server> dotnet-coverage shutdown serverdemo
D:\serverexample\server>
```

You can also start both server and client in background mode. Another process starts in the background and returns control back to the user.

Following is an example of full output in background server client mode:

```console
D:\serverexample\server> dotnet-coverage collect --session-id serverdemo --server-mode --background
D:\serverexample\server> dotnet-coverage connect --background serverdemo ConsoleApplication.exe World
D:\serverexample\server> dotnet-coverage connect --background serverdemo WpfApplication.exe
D:\serverexample\server> dotnet-coverage shutdown serverdemo
D:\serverexample\server>
```

## Static code coverage for managed assemblies

The dotnet-coverage tool can be used to collect code coverage for managed assemblies using static instrumentation. There are three different methods available that you can use. To demonstrate, let's assume we have a simple C# console application:

```console
D:\examples\ConsoleApp> dotnet run
Hello, World!
```

### Use collect command with include files option or configuration

If you don't want to use the `instrument` command, then the files to be instrumented can be specified using `--include-files` option as follows:

```console
D:\examples\ConsoleApp> dotnet-coverage collect --include-files .\bin\Debug\net9.0\*.dll dotnet run
dotnet-coverage v17.14.1.0 [win-x64 - .NET 9.0.2]

SessionId: 57862ec0-e512-49a5-8b66-2804174680fc
Hello, World!
Code coverage results: output.coverage.
```

You can also specify files to be instrumented using configuration as follows:

```xml
<ModulePaths>
  <IncludeDirectories>
    <Directory>D:\examples\ConsoleApp\bin\Debug\net7.0</Directory>
  </IncludeDirectories>
</ModulePaths>
```

### Using instrument and collect commands

In this case, first binary needs to be instrumented as follows:

```console
D:\examples\ConsoleApp> dotnet-coverage instrument .\bin\Debug\net7.0\ConsoleApp.dll
dotnet-coverage v17.14.1.0 [win-x64 - .NET 9.0.2]

Input file successfully instrumented.
```

Then you can collect code coverage as follows:

```console
D:\examples\ConsoleApp> dotnet-coverage collect .\bin\Debug\net7.0\ConsoleApp.exe
dotnet-coverage v17.14.1.0 [win-x64 - .NET 9.0.2]

SessionId: a09e6bef-ff64-4b5f-8bb8-fc495ebb50ba
Hello, World!
Code coverage results: output.coverage.
```

### Use the instrument and collect commands in server mode

In this case, you can completely separate coverage collection from running your application. First, instrument your binary as follows:

```console
D:\examples\ConsoleApp> dotnet-coverage instrument --session-id 73c34ce5-501c-4369-a4cb-04d31427d1a4 .\bin\Debug\net7.0\ConsoleApp.dll
dotnet-coverage v17.14.1.0 [win-x64 - .NET 9.0.2]

Input file successfully instrumented.
```

Note

Session ID needs to be used in this scenario to make sure that the application can connect and provide data to external collector.

In the second step, you need to start coverage collector as follows:

```console
D:\examples\ConsoleApp> dotnet-coverage collect --session-id 73c34ce5-501c-4369-a4cb-04d31427d1a4 --server-mode
dotnet-coverage v17.14.1.0 [win-x64 - .NET 9.0.2]

SessionId: 73c34ce5-501c-4369-a4cb-04d31427d1a4
```

Then the application can be started as follows:

```console
D:\examples\ConsoleApp> .\bin\Debug\net7.0\ConsoleApp.exe
Hello, World!
```

Finally, the collector can be closed as follows:

```console
D:\examples\ConsoleApp> dotnet-coverage shutdown 73c34ce5-501c-4369-a4cb-04d31427d1a4
dotnet-coverage v17.14.1.0 [win-x64 - .NET 9.0.2]
```

### Settings

You can specify a file with settings when you use the `collect` command. The settings file can be used to exclude some modules or methods from code coverage analysis. The format is the same as the data collector configuration inside a *runsettings* file. For more information, see [Customize code coverage analysis](/en-us/visualstudio/test/customizing-code-coverage-analysis). Here's an example:

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<Configuration>
    <CodeCoverage>
        <!--
        Additional paths to search for .pdb (symbol) files. Symbols must be found for modules to be instrumented.
        If .pdb files are in the same folder as the .dll or .exe files, they are automatically found. Otherwise, specify them here.
        Note that searching for symbols increases code coverage run time. So keep this small and local.
        -->
        <SymbolSearchPaths>
            <Path>C:\Users\User\Documents\Visual Studio 2012\Projects\ProjectX\bin\Debug</Path>
            <Path>\\mybuildshare\builds\ProjectX</Path>
        </SymbolSearchPaths>

        <!--
        About include/exclude lists:
        Empty "Include" clauses imply all; empty "Exclude" clauses imply none.
        Each element in the list is a regular expression (ECMAScript syntax). See /visualstudio/ide/using-regular-expressions-in-visual-studio.
        An item must first match at least one entry in the include list to be included.
        Included items must then not match any entries in the exclude list to remain included.
        -->

        <!-- Match assembly file paths: -->
        <ModulePaths>
            <Include>
                <ModulePath>.*\.dll$</ModulePath>
                <ModulePath>.*\.exe$</ModulePath>
            </Include>
            <Exclude>
                <ModulePath>.*CPPUnitTestFramework.*</ModulePath>
            </Exclude>
            <!-- Additional directories from .NET assemblies should be statically instrumented: -->
            <IncludeDirectories>
                <Directory Recursive="true">C:\temp</Directory>
            </IncludeDirectories>
        </ModulePaths>

        <!-- Match fully qualified names of functions: -->
        <!-- (Use "\." to delimit namespaces in C# or Visual Basic, "::" in C++.)  -->
        <Functions>
            <Exclude>
                <Function>^Fabrikam\.UnitTest\..*</Function>
                <Function>^std::.*</Function>
                <Function>^ATL::.*</Function>
                <Function>.*::__GetTestMethodInfo.*</Function>
                <Function>^Microsoft::VisualStudio::CppCodeCoverageFramework::.*</Function>
                <Function>^Microsoft::VisualStudio::CppUnitTestFramework::.*</Function>
            </Exclude>
        </Functions>

        <!-- Match attributes on any code element: -->
        <Attributes>
            <Exclude>
            <!-- Don't forget "Attribute" at the end of the name -->
                <Attribute>^System\.Diagnostics\.DebuggerHiddenAttribute$</Attribute>
                <Attribute>^System\.Diagnostics\.DebuggerNonUserCodeAttribute$</Attribute>
                <Attribute>^System\.CodeDom\.Compiler\.GeneratedCodeAttribute$</Attribute>
                <Attribute>^System\.Diagnostics\.CodeAnalysis\.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute$</Attribute>
            </Exclude>
        </Attributes>

        <!-- Match the path of the source files in which each method is defined: -->
        <Sources>
            <Exclude>
                <Source>.*\\atlmfc\\.*</Source>
                <Source>.*\\vctools\\.*</Source>
                <Source>.*\\public\\sdk\\.*</Source>
                <Source>.*\\microsoft sdks\\.*</Source>
                <Source>.*\\vc\\include\\.*</Source>
            </Exclude>
        </Sources>

        <!-- Match the company name property in the assembly: -->
        <CompanyNames>
            <Exclude>
                <CompanyName>.*microsoft.*</CompanyName>
            </Exclude>
        </CompanyNames>

        <!-- Match the public key token of a signed assembly: -->
        <PublicKeyTokens>
            <!-- Exclude Visual Studio extensions: -->
            <Exclude>
                <PublicKeyToken>^B77A5C561934E089$</PublicKeyToken>
                <PublicKeyToken>^B03F5F7F11D50A3A$</PublicKeyToken>
                <PublicKeyToken>^31BF3856AD364E35$</PublicKeyToken>
                <PublicKeyToken>^89845DCD8080CC91$</PublicKeyToken>
                <PublicKeyToken>^71E9BCE111E9429C$</PublicKeyToken>
                <PublicKeyToken>^8F50407C4E9E73B6$</PublicKeyToken>
                <PublicKeyToken>^E361AF139669C375$</PublicKeyToken>
            </Exclude>
        </PublicKeyTokens>

        <EnableStaticManagedInstrumentation>True</EnableStaticManagedInstrumentation>
        <EnableDynamicManagedInstrumentation>True</EnableDynamicManagedInstrumentation>

    </CodeCoverage>
</Configuration>
```

## Merge code coverage reports

You can merge `a.coverage` and `b.coverage` and store the data in `merged.coverage` as follows:

```console
dotnet-coverage merge -o merged.coverage a.coverage b.coverage
```

For example, if you run a command like `dotnet test --collect "Code Coverage"`, the coverage report is stored into a folder that is named a random GUID. Such folders are hard to find and merge. Using this tool, you can merge all code coverage reports for all your projects using globbing patterns as follows:

```console
dotnet-coverage merge -o merged.cobertura.xml -f cobertura **\*.coverage
```

The preceding command merges all coverage reports from the current directory and all subdirectories and stores the result into a cobertura file. In Azure Pipelines, you can use [Publish Code Coverage Results task](/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/tasks/test/publish-code-coverage-results) to publish a merged cobertura report.

You can use the `merge` command to convert a code coverage report to another format. For example, the following command converts a binary code coverage report into XML format.

```console
dotnet-coverage merge -o output.xml -f xml input.coverage
```

## Telemetry

Starting with version 18.10.0, the `dotnet-coverage` tool collects telemetry data to help Microsoft improve the code coverage tools. The data records which commands you run and which options you set when you run the tool. You can disable telemetry at any time. For more information about the data that's collected and how to opt out, see [Microsoft.CodeCoverage.Console telemetry](/en-us/visualstudio/test/microsoft-code-coverage-console-tool-telemetry).

display.text:
# применение clang-format ко всем C/C++ файлам репозитория
# проверка
# cmake -DMODE=check -DSRC_DIR=<корень> -DBUILD_DIR=<каталог сборки> -P cmake/format.cmake
# отформатировать
# cmake -DMODE=apply -DSRC_DIR=<корень> -DBUILD_DIR=<каталог сборки> -P cmake/format.cmake
# graceful decay - если на машине нет clang-format, об этом будет предупреждение, и тесты пройдут
# если есть но не отформатировано - будет падение

# проверка что режим передали
if(NOT DEFINED MODE OR (NOT "${MODE}" STREQUAL "check" AND NOT "${MODE}" STREQUAL "apply"))
    message(FATAL_ERROR "MODE must be 'check' or 'apply'; received: '${MODE}'")
endif()
# проверка что указали папку, в которой форматировать файлы
if(NOT DEFINED SRC_DIR OR "${SRC_DIR}" STREQUAL "")
    message(FATAL_ERROR "SRC_DIR is not set")
endif()
# по умолчанию каталог сборки - корень
if(NOT DEFINED BUILD_DIR)
    set(BUILD_DIR "")
endif()

# поиск clang-format-a
find_program(CLANG_FORMAT NAMES clang-format)

# если нет - предупреждаем и идём к тестам
if(NOT CLANG_FORMAT)
    message(WARNING "clang-format was not found, so the file format was not checked. Install it to enable this check: "
                    "winget install --id=LLVM.ClangFormat -e (Windows) / sudo apt install clang-format (Linux)")
    return()
endif()

# список проверяемых / форматируемых файлов
file(GLOB_RECURSE FORMAT_FILES
    "${SRC_DIR}/*.c"
    "${SRC_DIR}/*.cpp"
    "${SRC_DIR}/*.h"
    "${SRC_DIR}/*.hpp")

# исключить поддиректорию билда из ресурсов для фоматирования, т.к. там не программы, а их продукты 
# а также продукты генерации CMake - не надо форматировать этот код
# не дать исключить корень исходников, если кто-то соберёт "в корне"
if(NOT "${BUILD_DIR}" STREQUAL "" AND NOT "${BUILD_DIR}" STREQUAL "${SRC_DIR}")
    list(FILTER FORMAT_FILES EXCLUDE REGEX "^${BUILD_DIR}/")
endif()

# если нечего форматировать - кинуть предупреждение
if(FORMAT_FILES STREQUAL "")
    message(WARNING "No C/C++ source files found under ${SRC_DIR}")
    return()
endif()
# форматирование
if("${MODE}" STREQUAL "apply")
    execute_process(COMMAND "${CLANG_FORMAT}" -i ${FORMAT_FILES}
                    RESULT_VARIABLE result)
    if(NOT result EQUAL 0)
        message(FATAL_ERROR "clang-format failed to format the files (exit code ${result})")
    endif()
    message(STATUS "clang-format: files formatted")
# проверка формата
else()
    execute_process(COMMAND "${CLANG_FORMAT}" --dry-run -Werror ${FORMAT_FILES}
                    RESULT_VARIABLE result)
    if(NOT result EQUAL 0)
        message(FATAL_ERROR "clang-format found format violations. Run "
                            "'cmake --build <build-dir> --target format' to fix them, then re-run tests.")
    endif()
    message(STATUS "clang-format: file format is correct")
endif()

- Static native instrumentation requires `/PROFILE` link option, is recommended, and "will search and instrument all native binaries in directory where test binary is located" plus `IncludeDirectories`. Dynamic is always enabled by default; if static enabled and `/PROFILE`, static used.
- Settings format: full `<RunSettings>` or `<Configuration>` fragment (dotnet docs show `<Configuration><CodeCoverage>...`), or `<ModulePaths>` fragment (VS docs).
